Maximal regularity and optimal control for a non-local Cahn-Hilliard tumour growth model

Matteo Fornoni1
e-mail: matteo.fornoni01@universitadipavia.it

1Department of Mathematics "F. Casorati", Università degli Studi di Pavia,
via Ferrata 5, 27100, Pavia, Italy

Abstract

We consider a non-local tumour growth model of phase-field type, describing the evolution of tumour cells through proliferation in presence of a nutrient. The model consists of a coupled system, incorporating a non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation for the tumour phase variable and a reaction-diffusion equation for the nutrient. First, we establish novel regularity results for such a model, by applying maximal regularity theory in weighted LpL^{p} spaces. This technique enables us to prove the local existence and uniqueness of a regular solution, including also chemotaxis effects. By leveraging time-regularisation properties and global boundedness estimates, we further extend the solution to a global one. These results provide the foundation for addressing an optimal control problem, aimed at identifying a suitable therapy, guiding the tumour towards a predefined target. Specifically, we prove the existence of an optimal therapy and, by studying the Fréchet-differentiability of the control-to-state operator and introducing the adjoint system, we derive first-order necessary optimality conditions.

Key words: Non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation, Well-posedness, Maximal regularity, Optimal control, Tumour growth.

AMS (MOS) Subject Classification: 35K61, 45K05, 35B65, 35Q92, 49K20, 92C50.

1 Introduction

Mathematical modelling and analysis of tumour growth models is an expanding field that has been attracting much research in recent years. Indeed, it encompasses both modelling and numerical challenges, related to applicability with medical data (see [1, 8, 6, 25, 33, 34]), and analytical questions, related to well-posedness and regularity results (see [20, 43, 29, 27, 40]).

In the present paper, we consider a diffuse interface tumour growth model, which is a non-local variant of the one firstly introduced in [30]. In particular, it is a Cahn-Hilliard-based tumour growth model: for a general introduction to this type of models, we refer the reader to the recent review [24]. The key feature of diffuse interface models is the presence of a phase-field variable φ\varphi, representing the difference in volume fractions of tumour cells and healthy cells in a certain tissue. We assume that such variable can vary continuously between the tumour phase φ=1\varphi=1 and the healthy phase φ=−1\varphi=-1. Such approach, as opposed to a sharp-interface one, allows for an easier description of the tumour dynamics, both from an analytical and numerical point of view; additionally, topology changes in the tumour level set are also possible. In particular, the main object of our study is the following model:

∂tφ−div(m(φ)∇μ)=P(φ)(σ+χ(1−φ)−μ)−𝕙(φ)u\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi-\divergence(m(\varphi)\nabla\mu)=P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-\mu)-\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T},
μ=A​F′​(φ)+B​a​φ−B​J∗φ−χ​σ\displaystyle\mu=AF^{\prime}(\varphi)+Ba\varphi-BJ\ast\varphi-\chi\sigma\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T},
∂tσ−div(n(φ)∇(σ+χ(1−φ)))=−P(φ)(σ+χ(1−φ)−μ)+v\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma-\divergence(n(\varphi)\nabla(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)))=-P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-\mu)+v\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T},
m⁡(φ)​∂𝒏μ=n⁡(φ)​∂𝒏(σ+χ⁡(1−φ))=0\displaystyle m(\varphi)\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\mu=n(\varphi)\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi))=0\hskip 20.00003pt on ​ΣT,\displaystyle\text{on }\Sigma_{T},
φ⁡(0)=φ0,σ⁡(0)=σ0\displaystyle\varphi(0)=\varphi_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\sigma(0)=\sigma_{0}\hskip 20.00003pt in ​Ω,\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega,

where QT=Ω×(0,T)Q_{T}=\Omega\times(0,T), ΣT=∂Ω×(0,T)\Sigma_{T}=\partial\Omega\times(0,T) and Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, N=2,3N=2,3, is an open bounded sufficiently smooth domain, with exterior normal unit vector 𝒏\boldsymbol{n}.

We now briefly comment on the structure of the system. Other than φ\varphi, the second main variable of the system is σ\sigma, representing the concentration of a nutrient (e.g. oxygen or glucose), which is assumed to be the main consumable source used by the tumour cells to proliferate. As one can see, the phase-field variable φ\varphi satisfies a non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation, whereas σ\sigma satisfies a reaction-diffusion equation, and the two equations are non-trivially coupled through reaction terms and cross-diffusion ones, due to chemotactic effects. The non-locality is given by the convolution term B​a​φ−B​J∗φBa\varphi-BJ\ast\varphi in the equation for the chemical potential μ\mu associated to the Cahn-Hilliard equation. Throughout the paper, we call a=J∗1a=J\ast 1 (see also the forthcoming hypothesis A2). Including non-local effects is of paramount importance, for instance when modelling cell-to-cell adhesion effects (see [10]). The expression of μ\mu, as well as the form of the non-local terms, is deduced from the variational derivative of the Ginzburg-Landau free energy associated to the system:

ℰ⁡(φ,σ)=∫ΩA​F​(φ)​𝑑x+∫Ω∫ΩB4​J​(x−y)​(φ⁡(x)−φ⁡(y))2​𝑑x​𝑑y+∫Ω12|σ|2+χσ(1−φ)dx,\begin{split}\mathcal{E}(\varphi,\sigma)&=\int_{\Omega}AF(\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_{\Omega}\int_{\Omega}\frac{B}{4}J(x-y)(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y))^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\\ &\qquad+\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}\lvert\sigma\rvert^{2}+\chi\sigma(1-\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}x,\end{split} (1.1)

where A,B>0A,B>0 are parameters related to the width of the diffuse interface. We note that, without reaction terms and sources, the system above can be seen as an H−1H^{-1}-gradient flow of the previous free energy.

With this in mind, the first term in the free energy drives the evolution of the phase-field towards the minima of the function FF, which is typically taken as a double-well potential with equal minima in −1-1 and 11. Typical choices for such potential are for instance

Freg​(s)=14​(1−s2)2,s∈ℝ,\displaystyle F_{\text{reg}}(s)=\frac{1}{4}(1-s^{2})^{2},\hskip 10.00002pts\in\mathbb{R},
Fsing​(s)=θ2​[(1+s)​log⁡(1+s)+(1−s)​log⁡(1−s)]−θ02​s2,s∈(−1,1),0<θ<θ0,\displaystyle F_{\text{sing}}(s)=\frac{\theta}{2}\left[(1+s)\log(1+s)+(1-s)\log(1-s)\right]-\frac{\theta_{0}}{2}s^{2},\hskip 10.00002pts\in(-1,1),\hskip 10.00002pt0<\theta<\theta_{0},

From a modelling point of view, the best one would be the singular potential FsingF_{\text{sing}}. Indeed, its minima are strictly inside the interval (−1,1)(-1,1), but sufficiently close to the extrema, and its derivative blows up in ±1\pm 1. This still allows to restrict the evolution inside the physical interval [−1,1][-1,1], but also enables to show the existence of regular solutions, as long as a proper separation property is proved (see [26] for a recent overview on the matter, as well as [41]). In a few words, this amounts to proving that φ\varphi stays strictly inside the interval (−1,1)(-1,1) during its evolution, thus allowing free differentiation of the potential FsingF_{\text{sing}}. As such property is not always easy to prove, in many cases a suitable choice of the potential is the polynomial one FregF_{\text{reg}}, which, albeit not imposing the physical constraint, still typically guarantees good results in practice. Going back to the free energy (1.1), the second term is the one responsible for the non-local character of the model. Indeed, given a sufficiently regular symmetric convolution kernel JJ, typically of Newton or Bessel type, it can be seen as a non-local approximation of the standard Dirichlet energy that one would find for the local Cahn-Hilliard equation. From the modelling viewpoint, this term wants to penalise steep transitions between the two phases, in a non-local way. Indeed, if the kernel JJ is suitably peaked around zero, one can also recover the local model through asymptotic procedures (see [14, 16, 15]). Applications of the local Cahn-Hilliard equation to tumour growth problems have been widely studied, as one can see from the many articles already cited in this introduction, but the study of the non-local counterpart, where also some long-range interactions are considered, is just recently flourishing (see [25, 10, 44]). Our paper fits exactly in this framework. To conclude our commentary of the free energy (1.1), the third term is responsible for the nutrient diffusion mechanism and the fourth one for the chemotaxis effect, which is related to the natural movement of tumour cells towards regions with higher nutrient concentrations. Here we model chemotaxis through a cross-diffusion effect with intensity χ≥0\chi\geq 0, but more sophisticated models are also available, using for instance the celebrated Keller-Segel equations (see [43]).

Now, going back to our system, we comment on the remaining parameters. The functions m⁡(φ)m(\varphi) and n⁡(φ)n(\varphi) are called mobilities and regulate the diffusion processes of the two variables. In some cases, m⁡(φ)m(\varphi) can be taken degenerate in ±1\pm 1, like m⁡(φ)=1−φ2m(\varphi)=1-\varphi^{2}, to compensate the singularities of the potential FsingF_{\text{sing}} (see [23, 21]), but here we will work with the constant mobility case. The function P⁡(φ)P(\varphi), instead, is a proliferation function, calibrating the strength of the reaction terms, which, in turn, are written in this form due to chemical phenomenological laws (see [30]). Generally, it can be taken of the form P⁡(s)=max⁡{0,min⁡{12​(1+s),1}}P(s)=\max\{0,\min\{\frac{1}{2}(1+s),1\}\}, for s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, especially in case of young tumours, but other choices are also possible. To conclude, uu and vv are external sources that can be thought as medical therapies on the tumour: in particular, uu can be seen as radiotherapy acting directly on tumour cells and vv as a chemotherapy acting through the nutrient. In this case, the function 𝕙\mathbbm{h} is a bounded function that can be used to distribute the radiotherapy through particular strategies. In most cases, its expression would be similar to the one of PP.

The main purpose of this work is to analyse the previously introduced model with constant mobilities and regular potential. Indeed, we now assume m⁡(φ)=n⁡(φ)≡1m(\varphi)=n(\varphi)\equiv 1 for simplicity and consider FF to be a regular potential defined on the whole ℝ\mathbb{R}, satisfying certain hypotheses for which FregF_{\text{reg}} is certainly included (see the forthcoming hypotheses A3–A5). Hence, we actually consider the following system:

∂tφ−Δ​μ=P⁡(φ)​(σ+χ⁡(1−φ)−μ)−𝕙⁡(φ)​u\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi-\Delta\mu=P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-\mu)-\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}, (1.2)
μ=A​F′​(φ)+B​a​φ−B​J∗φ−χ​σ\displaystyle\mu=AF^{\prime}(\varphi)+Ba\varphi-BJ\ast\varphi-\chi\sigma\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}, (1.3)
∂tσ−Δ​σ+χ​Δ​φ=−P⁡(φ)​(σ+χ⁡(1−φ)−μ)+v\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma-\Delta\sigma+\chi\Delta\varphi=-P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-\mu)+v\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}, (1.4)

together with the following homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions and initial conditions:

∂𝒏μ=∂𝒏(σ−χ​φ)=0\displaystyle\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\mu=\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}(\sigma-\chi\varphi)=0\hskip 20.00003pt on ​ΣT,\displaystyle\text{on }\Sigma_{T}, (1.5)
φ⁡(0)=φ0,σ⁡(0)=σ0\displaystyle\varphi(0)=\varphi_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\sigma(0)=\sigma_{0}\hskip 20.00003pt in ​Ω.\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega. (1.6)

Our first main result concerns the existence and uniqueness of highly regular solutions to (1.2)–(1.6). To achieve this, we use an approach based on maximal regularity theory in weighted LpL^{p} spaces for parabolic equations with inhomogeneous Robin boundary conditions, as was recently done in [23] for a non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation with singular potential and degenerate mobility. The theory we apply was developed by M. Meyries and R. Schnaubelt in the series of papers [37, 38, 39], as well as the PhD thesis [36] of M. Meyries.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that such results are applied to a Cahn-Hilliard system with regular potential and constant mobilities, especially in presence of reaction terms, chemotaxis, external sources and space-dependent terms. In particular, the same procedure also guarantees new regularity results for the standard non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation with constant mobility and regular potential (see Remark 4.10). Indeed, other than the application of maximal regularity theory, the crucial point is to prove that weak solutions are globally bounded through an Alikakos-Moser iteration technique. On this point, we mention that this is an intrinsic problem related to the choice of a regular potential in the non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation. Opting for a singular potential, instead, would replace such problem with the hurdle of proving the aforementioned separation property. Great advances were made in [41], where such property was proved for the non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation in three space dimensions. Moreover, such results were later used in [42] to prove regularity results similar to ours in case of an advective non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation with constant mobility and singular potential. Let us mention, however, that their same procedure would not work in case of our tumour growth system, since the same proof of the separation property cannot be easily adapted to the presence of reaction terms. Finally, we observe that the Alikakos-Moser iteration scheme for our tumour growth system works only if we neglect the chemotaxis effect, i.e. we put χ=0\chi=0, since the low regularity of weak solutions is not enough to treat the cross-diffusion terms (see Proposition 4.1). Thus, we are actually able to prove local maximal regularity and uniqueness for the full model (see Theorem 3.10), but we are able to extend the local maximal solution to a global one only if χ=0\chi=0 (see Theorem 4.7). We stress that the local maximal regularity result of Theorem 3.10 holds also in the standard non-weighted case, that would be ρ=1\rho=1 in the setting of Section 3. However, one of the main ingredients for the extension to a global regular solution is the time-regularising effect of the weighted spaces, which allows to prove the key estimate contained in Lemma 3.11. For this reason, it is crucial to have maximal regularity in the time-weighted spaces to then recover a global regular solution even in the non-weighted case. To conclude this section about regularity, we just mention that our analysis was deeply inspired by [23], but in this work we chose to deal with the different case of regular potential and constant mobility. However, we strongly believe that all results on the tumour growth model should also easily extend to the case of singular potential and degenerate mobility as in [23]. In particular, also the application to the optimal control problem should be possible, by mimicking what was already done in [22].

Speaking of optimal control problems, we now introduce the second main goal of this paper, as well as the key reason why we strived to prove the existence of such regular solutions. Indeed, highly regular solutions of the tumour growth model are essentially needed if one wants to characterise the solutions to the optimal control problem through optimality conditions. In particular, the main step is to study in detail the differentiability properties of the control-to-state operator. Due to these reasons, to prove first order necessary conditions, we are forced to work in the chemotaxis-free case, meaning that we put χ=0\chi=0 and consider the system:

∂tφ−Δ​μ=P⁡(φ)​(σ−μ)−𝕙⁡(φ)​u\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi-\Delta\mu=P(\varphi)(\sigma-\mu)-\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}, (1.7)
μ=A​F′​(φ)+B​a​φ−B​J∗φ\displaystyle\mu=AF^{\prime}(\varphi)+Ba\varphi-BJ\ast\varphi\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}, (1.8)
∂tσ−Δ​σ=−P⁡(φ)​(σ−μ)+v\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma-\Delta\sigma=-P(\varphi)(\sigma-\mu)+v\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT.\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}. (1.9)
∂𝒏μ=∂𝒏σ=0\displaystyle\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\mu=\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\sigma=0\hskip 20.00003pt on ​ΣT,\displaystyle\text{on }\Sigma_{T}, (1.10)
φ⁡(0)=φ0,σ⁡(0)=σ0\displaystyle\varphi(0)=\varphi_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\sigma(0)=\sigma_{0}\hskip 20.00003pt in ​Ω.\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega. (1.11)

Our aim is to study the following optimal distributed control problem:

(CP) Minimise the cost functional

𝒥⁡(φ,σ,u,v)=αΩ2​∫Ω|φ⁡(T)−φΩ|2​𝑑x+αQ2​∫0T∫Ω|φ−φQ|2​𝑑x​𝑑t+βΩ2∫Ω|σ(T)−σΩ|2dx+βQ2∫0T∫Ω|σ−σQ|2dxdt+αu2∫0T∫Ω|u|2dxdt+βv2∫0T∫Ω|v|2dxdt,\begin{split}\mathcal{J}(\varphi,\sigma,u,v)&=\,\frac{\alpha_{\Omega}}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\varphi(T)-\varphi_{\Omega}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x+\frac{\alpha_{Q}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\varphi-\varphi_{Q}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\ &\quad+\frac{\beta_{\Omega}}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\sigma(T)-\sigma_{\Omega}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x+\frac{\beta_{Q}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\sigma-\sigma_{Q}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\ &\quad+\frac{\alpha_{u}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|u|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t+\frac{\beta_{v}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|v|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t,\end{split} (1.12)

subject to the control constraints

u∈𝒰ad:={u∈L∞​(QT)∣umin≤u≤umax​ a.e. in ​QT},v∈𝒱ad:={v∈L∞​(QT)∣vmin≤v≤vmax​ a.e. in ​QT},\begin{split}&u\in\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}:=\{u\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})\mid u_{\text{min}}\leq u\leq u_{\text{max}}\text{ a.e.\penalty\ in }Q_{T}\},\\ &v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{ad}}:=\{v\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})\mid v_{\text{min}}\leq v\leq v_{\text{max}}\text{ a.e.\penalty\ in }Q_{T}\},\end{split} (1.13)

and to the state system (1.7)-(1.11).

Here αΩ,αQ,βΩ,βQ,αu,βv\alpha_{\Omega},\alpha_{Q},\beta_{\Omega},\beta_{Q},\alpha_{u},\beta_{v} are non-negative parameters that can be used to select which targets have to be privileged. The function φΩ\varphi_{\Omega} is a final target for the tumour distribution, for instance one that could be suitable for surgery; whereas φQ\varphi_{Q} is a possibly desired evolution. In the same way, σΩ\sigma_{\Omega} and σQ\sigma_{Q} are respectively a final target and a desired evolution for the nutrient. Finally, the last two terms in the cost functional penalise large use of radiotherapy or chemotherapy, which could still harm the patient in the long run. The aim of the optimal control problem is, then, to find the best therapies uu and vv, which can lead the evolution of the tumour to the desired targets. Similar control problems for tumour growth models were studied in [12, 28, 13, 11, 9], but we can still count few contributions in the non-local case (see [22, 17, 43]). Regarding (CP), in Theorem 5.2 we show the existence of an optimal pair (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\overline{v}). Then, through careful analysis of the control-to-state operator and the introduction of the adjoint system, in Theorem 5.9 we prove the first-order necessary optimality conditions, which have to be satisfied by the optimal pair. We stress that proving necessary optimality conditions is the first step needed in order to justify numerical treatment of the optimal control problem. Indeed, the most commonly used algorithms are gradient descent schemes, where the descent direction is found through the optimality condition (see [45, Section 3.7] and references therein).

We finally mention that the present paper can be seen as a follow-up to [17], where the same optimal control problem for a similar model was analysed. The model in [17] is essentially the same as (1.2)–(1.6), up to an extra viscous regularisation term τ​∂tφ\tau\partial_{t}\varphi in (1.3) with τ>0\tau>0. The viscous term made it easier to prove high regularity results for the relaxed system, even with singular potentials and chemotaxis, however this called for an additional constraint on the control uu, namely it was necessary to assume that uu was uniformly bounded in H1​(0,T,L2​(Ω))H^{1}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)). Such additional constraint is definitely not a desired one in practice, as it makes it harder to compute the L2L^{2}-orthogonal projection onto 𝒰ad\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}, which is something that necessarily has to be done when solving numerically. In the present case, not only are we able to solve the optimal control problem without the viscous relaxation, but we are also able to avoid asking additional regularity on uu. This is mainly due to our new strategy for proving high regularity for the solution of the tumour growth model, relying on maximal regularity theory. We also mention that such theory was actually crucial in proving regularity results for our system in three dimensions. Indeed, our initial attempts made use of more standard techniques, inspired by [19], but they only got us a regular solution in two dimension without chemotaxis, while also assuming u∈H1​(0,T,L2​(Ω))u\in H^{1}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)).

The plan of the paper is the following. In Section 2, we state the notations and the main hypotheses on the parameters that will be used throughout the paper. Then, we state a first result about existence of weak solutions for (1.2)–(1.6), which directly follows from the results proven in [21]. In Section 3, we start by introducing all the machinery of maximal regularity theory in weighted LpL^{p} spaces and apply it to prove the first main result of the paper: Theorem 3.10 about local existence and uniqueness of maximal solutions, even for χ>0\chi>0. Moreover, we prove a technical result (Lemma 3.11) about a time-regularisation effect due to the use of weighted spaces, which is the key ingredient allowing the extension to a global solution. Section 4 is dedicated to proving strong well-posedness for the chemotaxis-free system (1.7)–(1.11). First, starting from weak solutions, we prove global boundedness through an Alikakos-Moser iteration scheme (Proposition 4.1) and a global Hölder regularity result (Proposition 4.5). Using these and the previous Lemma 3.11, we hence prove the second main result of the paper about existence and uniqueness of global highly regular solutions (Theorems 4.7 and 4.8). Finally, in Theorem 4.11 we prove a strong continuous dependence result from data, which is the first key step in the analysis of the optimal control problem. In Section 5, we consequently study the optimal control problem (CP). Indeed, we first prove existence of a solution in Theorem 5.2. Then, we consider the linearised system and prove the Fréchet-differentiability of the control-to-state operator in Theorem 5.5. In conclusion, we introduce the related adjoint system and deduce the first-order necessary optimality conditions in Theorem 5.9, the third main result of the paper.

2 Preliminaries and existence of weak solutions

We now introduce some notation that will be used throughout the paper. We denote with Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, N=2,3N=2,3 an open bounded domain with boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega of class 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2} and exterior normal unit vector 𝒏\boldsymbol{n}, whereas T>0T>0 is a fixed final time. The 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2} requirement for ∂Ω\partial\Omega is needed for regularity estimates in Section 3, while for weak solutions one can just assume that ∂Ω\partial\Omega is Lipschitz. For convenience, we also denote Qt=Ω×(0,t)Q_{t}=\Omega\times(0,t) and Σt=∂Ω×(0,t)\Sigma_{t}=\partial\Omega\times(0,t), for any t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T].

Next, we recall the usual conventions regarding the Hilbertian triplet used in this context. If we define

H=L2​(Ω),V=H1​(Ω),W={u∈H2​(Ω)∣∂𝒏u=0​ on ​∂Ω},H=L^{2}(\Omega),\hskip 10.00002ptV=H^{1}(\Omega),\hskip 10.00002ptW=\{u\in H^{2}(\Omega)\mid\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}u=0\text{ on }\partial\Omega\},

then we have the continuous and dense embeddings:

W↪V↪H≅H∗↪V∗↪W∗.W\hookrightarrow V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^{*}\hookrightarrow V^{*}\hookrightarrow W^{*}.

We denote by ⟨⋅,⋅⟩V\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V} the duality pairing between V∗V^{*} and VV and by (⋅,⋅)H(\cdot,\cdot)_{H} the scalar product in HH. Regarding Lebesgue and Sobolev spaces, we will use the notation ∥⋅∥Lp​(Ω)\lVert\cdot\rVert_{L^{p}(\Omega)} for the Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega)-norm and ∥⋅∥Wk,p​(Ω)\lVert\cdot\rVert_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)} for the Wk,p​(Ω)W^{k,p}(\Omega)-norm, with k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty. Moreover, we observe that, by elliptic regularity theory, an equivalent norm on WW is

∥u∥W2=∥u∥H2+∥Δ​u∥H2.\lVert u\rVert^{2}_{W}=\lVert u\rVert^{2}_{H}+\lVert\Delta u\rVert^{2}_{H}.

Finally, we recall the Riesz isomorphism 𝒩:V→V∗\mathcal{N}:V\to V^{*}:

⟨𝒩​u,v⟩V:=∫Ω(∇u⋅∇v+u​v)​𝑑x∀u,v∈V.\langle\mathcal{N}u,v\rangle_{V}:=\int_{\Omega}\left(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+uv\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\hskip 10.00002pt\forall u,v\in V.

It is well-known that for u∈Wu\in W we have 𝒩​u=−Δ​u+u∈H\mathcal{N}u=-\Delta u+u\in H and that the restriction of 𝒩\mathcal{N} to WW is an isomorphism from WW to HH. Additionally, by the spectral theorem, there exists a sequence of eigenvalues 0<λ1≤λ2≤…0<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\dots, with λj→+∞\lambda_{j}\to+\infty, and a family of eigenfunctions wj∈Ww_{j}\in W such that 𝒩​wj=λj​wj\mathcal{N}w_{j}=\lambda_{j}w_{j}, which forms an orthonormal basis in HH and an orthogonal basis in VV. In particular, w1w_{1} is constant.

Finally, we recall some useful inequalities that will be used throughout the paper:

    Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. Let Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} bounded Lipschitz, m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, 1≤r,q≤∞1\leq r,q\leq\infty, j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N} with 0≤j≤m0\leq j\leq m and j/m≤α≤1j/m\leq\alpha\leq 1 such that

Now we introduce the structural assumptions on the parameters of our model (1.2)–(1.6), which we recall here for convenience:

∂tφ−Δ​μ=P⁡(φ)​(σ+χ⁡(1−φ)−μ)−𝕙⁡(φ)​u\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi-\Delta\mu=P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-\mu)-\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T},

We assume the following:

  1. A1.

    A,B>0A,B>0 and χ≥0\chi\geq 0.

    and also that we have the bounds:

Finally, we would like to stress that, in the following, we will extensively use the symbol C>0C>0 to denote positive constants, which may change from line to line. They will depend only on Ω\Omega, TT, the parameters and on the norms of the fixed functions introduced in hypotheses A1–A9 and possible subsequent ones. Sometimes, we will also add subscripts on CC to highlight some particular dependences of these constants.

We now state a first result about existence of weak solutions to our system (1.2)–(1.6). We would like to point out that existence of weak solutions under assumptions A1–A9 was already proved in [21], when u≡v≡0u\equiv v\equiv 0. In our case, the presence of vv does not hinder the cited proof, since it can be easily treated. However, the term −𝕙⁡(φ)​u-\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u requires some little changes in said proof, by following what was done in [17, Remark 2.7]. Below we give just a brief idea on how to modify the argument, by leaving most of the details to the interested reader.

Theorem 2.1.

Under assumptions A1–A9, there exists a weak solution (φ,μ,σ)(\varphi,\mu,\sigma) to (1.2)–(1.6), such that

φ∈H1​(0,T,V∗)∩𝒞0​([0,T],H)∩L2​(0,T,V),\displaystyle\varphi\in H^{1}(0,T;V^{*})\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T],H)\cap L^{2}(0,T;V),
μ∈L2​(0,T,V),\displaystyle\mu\in L^{2}(0,T;V),
σ∈H1​(0,T,V∗)∩𝒞0​([0,T],H)∩L2​(0,T,V),\displaystyle\sigma\in H^{1}(0,T;V^{*})\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T],H)\cap L^{2}(0,T;V),

which satisfies

φ⁡(0)=φ0andσ⁡(0)=σ0in ​H\varphi(0)=\varphi_{0}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\sigma(0)=\sigma_{0}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{in }H

and the following variational formulation for a.e. t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T) and for any ζ∈V\zeta\in V:

⟨φt,ζ⟩V+(∇μ,∇ζ)H=(P⁡(φ)​(σ+χ⁡(1−φ)−μ),ζ)H−(𝕙⁡(φ)​u,ζ)H,\displaystyle\langle\varphi_{t},\zeta\rangle_{V}+(\nabla\mu,\nabla\zeta)_{H}=(P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-\mu),\zeta)_{H}-(\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u,\zeta)_{H}, (2.3)
(μ,ζ)H=(A​F′​(φ)+B​a​φ−B​J∗φ−χ​σ,ζ)H,\displaystyle(\mu,\zeta)_{H}=(AF^{\prime}(\varphi)+Ba\varphi-BJ\ast\varphi-\chi\sigma,\zeta)_{H}, (2.4)
⟨σt,ζ⟩V+(∇σ−χ∇φ,∇ζ)H=−(P(φ)(σ+χ(1−φ)−μ),ζ)H+⟨v,ζ⟩V.\displaystyle\langle\sigma_{t},\zeta\rangle_{V}+(\nabla\sigma-\chi\nabla\varphi,\nabla\zeta)_{H}=-(P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-\mu),\zeta)_{H}+\langle v,\zeta\rangle_{V}. (2.5)

In particular, there exists a constant C>0C>0, depending only on the parameters of the model and on the data φ0\varphi_{0}, σ0\sigma_{0}, uu and vv, such that:

∥φ∥H1​(0,T,V∗)∩L∞​(0,T,H)∩L2​(0,T,V)+∥μ∥L2​(0,T,V)+∥σ∥H1​(0,T,V∗)∩L∞​(0,T,H)∩L2​(0,T,V)≤C.\begin{split}&\lVert\varphi\rVert_{H^{1}(0,T;V^{*})\cap L^{\infty}(0,T,H)\cap L^{2}(0,T;V)}+\lVert\mu\rVert_{L^{2}(0,T;V)}\\ &\quad+\lVert\sigma\rVert_{H^{1}(0,T;V^{*})\cap L^{\infty}(0,T,H)\cap L^{2}(0,T;V)}\leq C.\end{split} (2.6)
Proof.

The proof follows exactly the argument of [21, Theorem 2.1], with one main difference due to the presence of the source terms. The main energy estimate is done by testing (1.2) by μ\mu, (1.3) by −φt-\varphi_{t} and (1.4) by σ+χ⁡(1−φ)\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi). Therefore, the two extra terms to treat are −(𝕙⁡(φ)​u,μ)H-(\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u,\mu)_{H} and ⟨v,σ+χ⁡(1−φ)⟩V\langle v,\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)\rangle_{V}. The second one can be easily treated by duality properties and Young’s inequality. Regarding the first one, instead, one can argue exactly as in the first part of [17, Remark 2.7], by assuming τ=0\tau=0. Observe that, in this case, one also has to slightly modify the estimate from below of the energy E⁡(t)E(t) as in [17, Remark 2.7]. In this way, the bound F⁡(φ)∈L∞​(0,T,L1​(Ω))F(\varphi)\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{1}(\Omega)) directly comes from the first energy estimate.

The rest of the procedure, also including the Galerkin approximation and the passage to the limit, is the same as [21, Theorem 2.1], so we omit the details. ∎

3 Local Maximal LρpL^{p}_{\rho} regularity

As already stated in the introduction, in order to prove further regularity for the solutions of our system (1.2)-(1.6), we use an approach based on maximal regularity theory in weighted LpL^{p} spaces. Before starting, we recall some notation and results introduced in the series of papers [37, 38, 39]. Then, we apply their results to prove local existence and uniqueness of maximal solutions. In our case, the difference from the previous works is that we are dealing with a system of equations containing also some space-dependent and time-dependent terms, as well as some external source terms. Therefore we have to make some adjustments, but the core of the argument is similar to the one of [23].

3.1 Functional framework

We start by introducing the function spaces that we are going to use and by reformulating our problem (1.2)-(1.6) in a more suitable way. Following [38], for p∈(1,+∞)p\in(1,+\infty), ρ∈(1/p,1]\rho\in(1/p,1], XX real Banach space and T∈(0,+∞)T\in(0,+\infty), we introduce the time-weighted spaces:

Lρp(0,T;X):={f:(0,T)→X strongly measurable such that \displaystyle L^{p}_{\rho}(0,T;X):=\Big\{f:(0,T)\to X\hbox{ strongly measurable such that }
∥f∥Lρp​(0,T,X)p=∫0Ttp⁡(1−ρ)∥f(t)∥Xpdt<+∞},\displaystyle\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 20.00003pt\lVert f\rVert^{p}_{L^{p}_{\rho}(0,T;X)}=\int_{0}^{T}t^{p(1-\rho)}\lVert f(t)\rVert_{X}^{p}\,\mathrm{d}t<+\infty\Big\},
Wρ1,p​(0,T,X):={f∈Lρp​(0,T,X)∣∂tf∈Lρp​(0,T,X)}.\displaystyle W^{1,p}_{\rho}(0,T;X):=\left\{f\in L^{p}_{\rho}(0,T;X)\mid\partial_{t}f\in L^{p}_{\rho}(0,T;X)\right\}.

Observe that ρ=1\rho=1 yields the unweighted case, which means that L1p=LpL^{p}_{1}=L^{p}, moreover one can easily see that Lp​(0,T,X)↪Lρp​(0,T,X)L^{p}(0,T;X)\hookrightarrow L^{p}_{\rho}(0,T;X) for any ρ∈(1/p,1]\rho\in(1/p,1]. Then, in a standard way, one can define the spaces Wρk,p​(0,T,X)W^{k,p}_{\rho}(0,T;X) for any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and, by real interpolation, also the fractional order spaces Wρs,p​(0,T,X)W^{s,p}_{\rho}(0,T;X) for any s∈ℝ+s\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, as done in [38].

Remark 3.1.

We observe that the temporal weight tp⁡(1−ρ)t^{p(1-\rho)} has a regularising effect only for t=0t=0. Namely, if f∈Lρp​(0,T,Lp​(Ω))f\in L^{p}_{\rho}(0,T;L^{p}(\Omega)) with ρ∈(1/p,1]\rho\in(1/p,1], then f∈L1p​(s,T,Lp​(Ω))f\in L^{p}_{1}(s,T;L^{p}(\Omega)) for any s>0s>0. Indeed:

+∞>∫sTtp⁡(1−ρ)​∥f∥Lp​(Ω)p​𝑑t≥(min[s,T]⁡tp⁡(1−ρ))​∫sT∥f∥Lp​(Ω)p​𝑑t⟹∫sT∥f∥Lp​(Ω)p​𝑑t<+∞.+\infty>\int_{s}^{T}t^{p(1-\rho)}\lVert f\rVert^{p}_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\,\mathrm{d}t\geq\left(\min_{[s,T]}t^{p(1-\rho)}\right)\int_{s}^{T}\lVert f\rVert^{p}_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\,\mathrm{d}t\implies\int_{s}^{T}\lVert f\rVert^{p}_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\,\mathrm{d}t<+\infty.

However, this is enough to prove some useful time-regularisation estimates (see Lemma 3.11).

From now on, we assume that the bounded domain Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, N=2,3N=2,3, has boundary of class 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2}. Next, we introduce the actual spaces we work with for our maximal regularity theory. Let I=(0,T)I=(0,T) be a finite time-interval, p∈(N+2,+∞)p\in(N+2,+\infty) and ρ∈(1/p,1]\rho\in(1/p,1]. We define the maximal regularity class

E2,ρ​(I):=Wρ1,p​(I,Lp​(Ω))∩Lρp​(I,W2,p​(Ω)),E_{2,\rho}(I):=W^{1,p}_{\rho}(I;L^{p}(\Omega))\cap L^{p}_{\rho}(I;W^{2,p}(\Omega)),

the boundary class

Fρ​(I):=Wρ12−12​p,p​(I,Lp​(∂Ω))∩Lρp​(I,W1−1p,p​(∂Ω)),F_{\rho}(I):=W^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2p},\,p}_{\rho}(I;L^{p}(\partial\Omega))\cap L^{p}_{\rho}(I;W^{1-\frac{1}{p},\,p}(\partial\Omega)),

as well as the starting space

E0,ρ​(I)=Lρp​(I,Lp​(Ω)).E_{0,\rho}(I)=L^{p}_{\rho}(I;L^{p}(\Omega)).

Note that, for the boundary class, we are dealing with Neumann boundary conditions, therefore it is expected that the spaces have one degree less of regularity with respect to Dirichlet trace spaces. We recall that, regarding these spaces, in [38] the following embedding results were proved:

E2,ρ​(I)↪𝒞0​(I¯,W2​(ρ−1p),p​(Ω))↪𝒞0​(I¯,𝒞1​(Ω¯)),E_{2,\rho}(I)\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}^{0}(\overline{I},W^{2\left(\rho-\frac{1}{p}\right),\,p}(\Omega))\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}^{0}(\overline{I},\mathcal{C}^{1}(\overline{\Omega})), (3.1)

where the last embedding holds if and only if 2​(ρ−1p)>1+Np2\left(\rho-\frac{1}{p}\right)>1+\frac{N}{p}. Moreover, if 2​(ρ−1p)>1+1p2\left(\rho-\frac{1}{p}\right)>1+\frac{1}{p}, we also have that

Fρ​(I)↪𝒞0​(I¯,W2​(ρ−1p)−1−1p,p​(∂Ω))↪𝒞0​(I¯,𝒞0​(∂Ω)),F_{\rho}(I)\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}^{0}(\overline{I},W^{2\left(\rho-\frac{1}{p}\right)-1-\frac{1}{p},\,p}(\partial\Omega))\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}^{0}(\overline{I},\mathcal{C}^{0}(\partial\Omega)), (3.2)

where again the last embedding holds if and only if 2​(ρ−1p)>1+Np2\left(\rho-\frac{1}{p}\right)>1+\frac{N}{p}.

Now, it is convenient to rewrite our system (1.2)-(1.6) in the following abstract form:

∂t𝛙⁡(x,t)+𝒜⁡(x,t,𝛙⁡(x,t))=𝒗⁡(x,t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(x,t)+\mathcal{A}\left(x,t,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(x,t)\right)=\boldsymbol{v}(x,t)\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T},
ℬ⁡(x,𝛙⁡(x,t))=𝟎\displaystyle\mathcal{B}\left(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(x,t)\right)=\boldsymbol{0}\hskip 20.00003pt on ​ΣT,\displaystyle\text{on }\Sigma_{T}, (3.3)
𝛙⁡(x,0)=𝛙0​(x)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(x,0)=\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}(x)\hskip 20.00003pt in ​Ω,\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega,

where

𝛙⁡(x,t)=(φ⁡(x,t)σ⁡(x,t)),𝛙0​(x)=(φ0​(x)σ0​(x)),𝒜⁡(x,t,𝛙)=(𝒜1​(x,t,φ,σ)𝒜2​(x,φ,σ)),\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(x,t)=\binom{\varphi(x,t)}{\sigma(x,t)},\hskip 10.00002pt\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}(x)=\binom{\varphi_{0}(x)}{\sigma_{0}(x)},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{A}\left(x,t,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}\right)=\binom{\mathcal{A}_{1}(x,t,\varphi,\sigma)}{\mathcal{A}_{2}(x,\varphi,\sigma)},

with components given by

𝒜1(x,t,φ,σ)=−div((AF′′(φ)+Ba(x))∇φ)+χΔσ−div(B∇a(x)φ−B∇J∗φ)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{1}(x,t,\varphi,\sigma)=-\divergence((AF^{\prime\prime}(\varphi)+Ba(x))\nabla\varphi)+\chi\Delta\sigma-\divergence(B\nabla a(x)\,\varphi-B\nabla J\ast\varphi)
−P⁡(φ)​(σ+χ⁡(1−φ)−A​F′​(φ)−B​a​(x)​φ+B​J∗φ+χ​σ)+𝕙⁡(φ)​u​(x,t),\displaystyle\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 10.00002pt-P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-AF^{\prime}(\varphi)-Ba(x)\,\varphi+BJ\ast\varphi+\chi\sigma)+\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u(x,t),
𝒜2​(x,φ,σ)=−Δ​σ+χ​Δ​φ\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{2}(x,\varphi,\sigma)=-\Delta\sigma+\chi\Delta\varphi
+P⁡(φ)​(σ+χ⁡(1−φ)−A​F′​(φ)−B​a​(x)​φ+B​J∗φ+χ​σ)\displaystyle\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 10.00002pt+P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-AF^{\prime}(\varphi)-Ba(x)\,\varphi+BJ\ast\varphi+\chi\sigma)

and

ℬ⁡(x,𝛙)=(∇φ∣∂Ω⋅𝒏+l(x,φ∣∂Ω)(Bφ∣∂Ω∇a(x)⋅𝒏−B(∇J∗φ)∣∂Ω⋅𝒏−χ∇σ∣∂Ω⋅𝒏)∇σ∣∂Ω⋅𝒏−χ∇φ∣∂Ω⋅𝒏),\mathcal{B}\left(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}\right)=\binom{\nabla\varphi_{\mid\partial\Omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}+l(x,\varphi_{\mid\partial\Omega})\left(B\varphi_{\mid\partial\Omega}\nabla a(x)\cdot\boldsymbol{n}-B(\nabla J\ast\varphi)_{\mid\partial\Omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}-\chi\nabla\sigma_{\mid\partial\Omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}\right)}{\nabla\sigma_{\mid\partial\Omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}-\chi\nabla\varphi_{\mid\partial\Omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}},

with

0≤l⁡(x,s):=1A​F′′​(s)+B​a​(x)≤1c0for a.e. ​x∈Ω​ and any ​s∈ℝ,0\leq l(x,s):=\frac{1}{AF^{\prime\prime}(s)+Ba(x)}\leq\frac{1}{c_{0}}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{for a.e. }x\in\Omega\text{ and any }s\in\mathbb{R},

and finally

𝒗⁡(x,t)=(0v⁡(x,t)).\hskip 10.00002pt\boldsymbol{v}(x,t)=\binom{0}{v(x,t)}.
Remark 3.2.

We want to stress that our operators 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} depend also on xx and tt, differently from what was done in [37] and [23]. However, the dependence on xx is only through the function a∈W1,∞​(Ω)a\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega) (actually, we will have a∈W2,q​(Ω)a\in W^{2,q}(\Omega), for any q>1q>1, with additional hypotheses on JJ; see Remark 3.7 in the next subsection). The dependence on tt, instead, is only through the function u⁡(x,t)∈L∞​(QT)u(x,t)\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T}), which appears only as a lower order term. Moreover, we also have a source term, which we will assume to be 𝒗∈L∞​(QT)2\boldsymbol{v}\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})^{2}. Consequently, the high regularity of these terms allows us to proceed with similar arguments to the ones used in the cited papers, up to some adjustments.

Remark 3.3.

Observe that, by hypothesis A3, the function l⁡(x,s)l(x,s) is well-defined for any s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} and for a.e. x∈Ωx\in\Omega. Moreover, if F∈𝒞4​(ℝ)F\in\mathcal{C}^{4}(\mathbb{R}), we also have that

l⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒞2​(ℝ)for a.e. ​x∈Ω.l(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R})\hskip 10.00002pt\text{for a.e. }x\in\Omega.

We additionally remark that we chose to rewrite the first boundary condition in (1.5) by using the function l(x,φ∣∂Ω)l(x,\varphi_{\mid\partial\Omega}) in order to highlight the structure of an inhomogeneous Robin boundary condition and to keep consistency with the notation used in [23].

Finally, we introduce the sought regularity for the solutions of (3.3):

Definition 3.4.

Assume that the initial data belong to the following space:

𝛙0∈Ms,p:={𝛙∈(Ws,p​(Ω))2∣ℬ⁡(x,𝛙)=0​ a.e. on ​Ω},\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}\in M^{s,p}:=\{\boldsymbol{\uppsi}\in(W^{s,p}(\Omega))^{2}\mid\mathcal{B}(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi})=0\text{ a.e. on }\Omega\},

with

p∈(N+2,+∞),ρ∈(12+N+22​p,1], and s=2(ρ−1p)>1+Np.p\in(N+2,+\infty),\hskip 10.00002pt\rho\in\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{N+2}{2p},1\right],\hskip 10.00002pt\text{ and }s=2\left(\rho-\frac{1}{p}\right)>1+\frac{N}{p}.

We say that 𝛙\boldsymbol{\uppsi} is a maximal solution to (3.3) on the interval I=(0,T)I=(0,T) if it satisfies (3.3) almost everywhere in QTQ_{T} and

𝛙∈(E2,ρ​(I))2∩𝒞0​([0,T),Ms,p).\boldsymbol{\uppsi}\in(E_{2,\rho}(I))^{2}\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T);M^{s,p}).
Remark 3.5.

One could also be interested in studying existence of maximal solutions for all times, i.e. for T=+∞T=+\infty. Indeed, this can easily be included in our theory by considering weighted spaces with zero temporal trace in t=0t=0. More details about this matter can be found in the already cited papers [37, 39, 23]. In particular, in [37] it was shown that, for this kind of zero temporal trace spaces, the constants of the embeddings 3.1 and 3.2 are independent of T>0T>0. However, for simplicity we will stick with finite-time evolution.

3.2 Local-in-time existence

The aim of this subsection is to establish existence and uniqueness of maximal solutions to (3.3), in the sense of Definition 3.4, at least locally in time, by adapting the results proved in [39, 37]. In order to prove this, we shall use maximal LρpL^{p}_{\rho}-regularity results for the linearised problem associated to (3.3) and then apply the Banach contraction principle to get the same regularity also in the non-linear case. We observe that, as it is said in [37, Remark 3.6], as long as the operators 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} are of class 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} and a version of the maximal LρpL^{p}_{\rho}-regularity holds for the corresponding linearised problem, the proof of local existence and uniqueness is actually independent of the concrete form of the operators. Therefore, by looking at [39, Theorem 2.1] for maximal regularity for linear parabolic systems, we can include also our (x,t)(x,t)-dependent operators in this setting.

We now need to assume stronger hypotheses on the parameters of our system (1.2)-(1.6), on top of the previous ones. In particular, we would need to assume that J∈Wloc2,1​(ℝN)J\in W^{2,1}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{N}), but this hypothesis is incompatible with widely used convolution kernels, such as those of Newton or Bessel type. However, following [5, Definition 1], we can still introduce a suitable class of kernels, which includes the ones mentioned before and satisfies our needs. Indeed, we recall the following definition:

Definition 3.6.

A convolution kernel J∈Wloc1,1​(ℝN)J\in W^{1,1}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) is admissible if it satisfies the following conditions:

  • •

    J∈𝒞3​(ℝN∖{0})J\in\mathcal{C}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{N}\setminus\{0\}).

  • •

    JJ is radially symmetric and non-increasing, i.e. J​(⋅)=J~​(|⋅|)J(\cdot)=\tilde{J}(\lvert\cdot\rvert) for a non-increasing function J~:ℝ+→ℝ\tilde{J}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}.

  • •

    There exists R0R_{0} such that r↦J~′′​(r)r\mapsto\tilde{J}^{\prime\prime}(r) and r↦J~′​(r)/rr\mapsto\tilde{J}^{\prime}(r)/r are monotone on (0,R0)(0,R_{0}).

  • •

    There exists CN>0C_{N}>0 such that |D3​J​(x)|≤CN​|x|−N−1\lvert D^{3}J(x)\rvert\leq C_{N}\lvert x\rvert^{-N-1} for any x∈ℝ3∖{0}x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\}.

Now, we can assume the following:

  1. B1.

    J∈Wloc2,1​(ℝN)J\in W^{2,1}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) or JJ is admissible in the sense of Definition 3.6.

  2. B2.

    F∈𝒞4​(ℝ)F\in\mathcal{C}^{4}(\mathbb{R}).

  3. B3.

    P∈𝒞1​(ℝ)P\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\mathbb{R}).

  4. B4.

    𝕙∈𝒞1​(ℝ)\mathbbm{h}\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\mathbb{R}).

  5. B5.

    u,v∈L∞​(QT)u,v\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T}).

  6. B6.

    𝛙0=(φ0σ0)∈Ms,p\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}=\displaystyle\binom{\varphi_{0}}{\sigma_{0}}\in M^{s,p} as in Definition 3.4.

Remark 3.7.

We recall that if JJ satisfies B1, then, by [5, Lemma 2], for any p∈(1,+∞)p\in(1,+\infty) there exists a constant bp>0b_{p}>0 such that:

∥∇(∇J∗f)∥Lp​(Ω)3×3≤bp∥f∥Lp​(Ω)∀f∈Lp(Ω).\lVert\nabla(\nabla J\ast f)\rVert_{L^{p}(\Omega)^{3\times 3}}\leq b_{p}\lVert f\rVert_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\hskip 10.00002pt\forall f\in L^{p}(\Omega).

Moreover, by Young’s inequality for convolutions, this implies that a∈W2,p​(Ω)a\in W^{2,p}(\Omega) for any p∈(1,+∞)p\in(1,+\infty). In this way we can include typical choices for JJ, such as Newton or Bessel type potentials, which satisfy Definition 3.6.

Before proving the main result, we state and prove two technical lemmas about the regularity of the operators 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}.

We immediately observe that ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} is linear, so there is nothing to prove regarding the second component. The only difficult part is the first component ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}, but in this case the proof is essentially identical to the one of [23, Lemma 3.3]. At this point, we can state and prove our main result about existence and uniqueness of local maximal solutions.

At this point, since we have a unique maximal solution for the linearised system, we can employ the Banach contraction principle, exactly as in [37, Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3], to find the required maximal solution 𝛙\boldsymbol{\uppsi} to (3.3). 𝛏⁡(x,0)=𝛙0​(x)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\upxi}(x,0)=\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}(x)\hskip 20.00003pt in ​Ω,\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega,

and observe that both the right-hand sides 𝒜′​(x,t,𝛙∗)​𝛙∗−𝒜⁡(x,t,𝛙∗)+𝒗∈E0,ρ​(I)\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\left(x,t,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{*}\right)\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{*}-\mathcal{A}(x,t,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{*})+\boldsymbol{v}\in E_{0,\rho}(I) and ℬ′​(x,𝛙∗)​𝛏=ℬ′​(x,𝛙∗)​𝛙∗−ℬ⁡(x,𝛙∗)∈Fρ​(I)\mathcal{B}^{\prime}\left(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{*}\right)\boldsymbol{\upxi}=\mathcal{B}^{\prime}\left(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{*}\right)\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{*}-\mathcal{B}(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{*})\in F_{\rho}(I) belong to the right spaces, due to Lemmas 3.8 and 3.9, and also, since ℬ⁡(𝛙0)=0\mathcal{B}(\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0})=0, the compatibility condition ℬ′​(x,𝛙0)​𝛙0=ℬ′​(x,𝛙0)​𝛙0−ℬ⁡(x,𝛙0)\mathcal{B}^{\prime}(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0})\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}=\mathcal{B}^{\prime}(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0})\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}-\mathcal{B}(x,\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}) on ∂Ω\partial\Omega holds. 𝛏⁡(x,0)=𝛙0​(x)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\upxi}(x,0)=\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}(x) in ​Ω.\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega.

Exactly as above, also this linear system admits a unique solution 𝛏=𝒮⁡(𝛙)∈E2,ρ​(0,τ)\boldsymbol{\upxi}=\mathcal{S}(\boldsymbol{\uppsi})\in E_{2,\rho}(0,\tau) and this defines a map 𝒮:Σ⁡(λ,τ)→E2,ρ​(0,τ)\mathcal{S}:\Sigma(\lambda,\tau)\to E_{2,\rho}(0,\tau). Clearly, 𝛙∈Σ⁡(λ,τ)\boldsymbol{\uppsi}\in\Sigma(\lambda,\tau) solves our starting system (3.3) if and only if it is a fixed point of 𝒮\mathcal{S} in Σ⁡(λ,τ)\Sigma(\lambda,\tau). Since, for given λ\lambda, each solution of (3.3) in E2,ρ​(0,τ)E_{2,\rho}(0,\tau) belongs to Σ⁡(λ,τ)\Sigma(\lambda,\tau) for sufficiently small τ\tau, our task is thus to show that the map 𝒮\mathcal{S} has a unique fixed point in Σ⁡(λ,τ)\Sigma(\lambda,\tau), provided that λ\lambda and τ\tau are sufficiently small. To this end we use the Banach contraction principle. Indeed, one has to show that 𝒮\mathcal{S} maps Σ⁡(λ,τ)\Sigma(\lambda,\tau) into itself for small λ\lambda and τ\tau, as well as that it is a contraction on Σ⁡(λ,τ)\Sigma(\lambda,\tau). These two properties can be verified exactly as in second and third steps of the proof of [36, Proposition 4.3.2], by relying on the inequalities proven in Lemmas 3.8 and 3.9 and on properties of zero-temporal-trace spaces (see Remark 3.5) to keep constants independent of τ\tau. The existence of a maximal existence time t+=t+​(𝛙0,𝒗)t^{+}=t^{+}(\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0},\boldsymbol{v}) and a maximal solution in 𝒞⁡([0;t+),Ws,p​(Ω,ℝN))\mathcal{C}([0;t^{+});W^{s,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{N})) then follows from standard arguments. ∎

We have shown that, under hypotheses A1-A7 and B1–B6, our system (1.2)-(1.6) admits a unique maximal solution with regularity

φ,σ∈E2,ρ​(0,t+):=Wρ1,p​(0,t+,Lp​(Ω))∩Lρp​(0,t+,W2,p​(Ω)),\varphi,\sigma\in E_{2,\rho}(0,t^{+}):=W^{1,p}_{\rho}(0,t^{+};L^{p}(\Omega))\cap L^{p}_{\rho}(0,t^{+};W^{2,p}(\Omega)),

with ρ∈(12+N+22​p,1]\rho\in\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{N+2}{2p},1\right] and p∈(N+2,+∞)p\in(N+2,+\infty), up to a certain maximal time t+=t+​(φ0,σ0)t^{+}=t^{+}(\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0}). In the next section, we will extend this regularity to the whole interval (0,T)(0,T), however, in order to do this, it will be necessary to put χ=0\chi=0. Before going into the details, we need another technical lemma about a 𝒞β−W2−2/p,p\mathcal{C}^{\beta}-W^{2-2/p,p} smoothing effect for the solutions to our problem, which will be useful in the next section. Note that this lemma can still be proven even if χ>0\chi>0.

Lemma 3.11.

Let ρ=1\rho=1, p∈(N+2,+∞)p\in(N+2,+\infty) and 𝛙0∈M2−2/p,p\boldsymbol{\uppsi}_{0}\in M^{2-2/p,p}. Assume also hypotheses A1-A7 and B1-B5.

Let 𝛙\boldsymbol{\uppsi} be a maximal solution to (3.3) on (0,t+)(0,t^{+}) in the sense of Definition 3.4 and let t1,t2∈(0,t+)t_{1},t_{2}\in(0,t^{+}), with t2>t1t_{2}>t_{1} and τ:=t2−t1\tau:=t_{2}-t_{1}. Then, for any β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), there exists a constant C>0C>0, depending only on the parameters of the system and τ\tau, pp and δβ=∥𝛙∥(𝒞​([t1,t2],𝒞β​(Ω))2𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸\delta_{\beta}=\lVert\boldsymbol{\uppsi}\rVert_{(\mathcal{C}([t_{1},t_{2}];\mathcal{C}^{\beta}(\Omega))^{2}}, such that

∥𝛙⁡(t2)∥(W2−2/p,p​(Ω))2≤C⁡(1+∥𝛙⁡(t1)∥(𝒞β​(Ω))2).\lVert\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(t_{2})\rVert_{(W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega))^{2}}\leq C(1+\lVert\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(t_{1})\rVert_{(\mathcal{C}^{\beta}(\Omega))^{2}}).
Remark 3.12.

The smoothing effect provided by this lemma will be crucial in establishing global regular solutions and it is actually the reason why we need to consider weighted spaces. Indeed, the regularisation effect of the time-weight is the crucial ingredient of the argument. This will be clear in the last part of the proof.

Proof.

We mostly follow the argument of [23, Lemma 3.5], which in turn is inspired by the one of [37, Lemma 4.1].

Now fix t1<t2∈(0,t+)t_{1}<t_{2}\in(0,t^{+}) and τ=t2−t1\tau=t_{2}-t_{1}. Given 𝛙\boldsymbol{\uppsi} maximal solution to (3.3), we define 𝛇⁡(t):=𝛙⁡(t+t1)\boldsymbol{\upzeta}(t):=\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(t+t_{1}) for any t∈(0,τ)t\in(0,\tau). Then, since 𝛙∈E2,1​(0,t+)\boldsymbol{\uppsi}\in E_{2,1}(0,t^{+}), we have that 𝛇∈E2,1​(0,τ)\boldsymbol{\upzeta}\in E_{2,1}(0,\tau). Moreover, we recall that 𝛙∈E2,1​(0,t+)↪𝒞0​(0,t+,W2−2/p,p​(Ω))\boldsymbol{\uppsi}\in E_{2,1}(0,t^{+})\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}^{0}(0,t^{+};W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega)) by (3.1) with ρ=1\rho=1, hence this implies that

where the last inequality holds for any ρ∈(1/p,1]\rho\in(1/p,1], due to Remark 3.1. Note that here we passed from the unweighted case to the weighted one, in order to exploit the time-regularisation effect. Now, observe that, by definition, 𝛇=(ξθ)\boldsymbol{\upzeta}=\binom{\xi}{\theta} satisfies the following system of partial differential equations:

are normally elliptic and satisfy the Lopatinskii-Shapiro type condition. Again, both conditions can be verified by applying [2, Theorem 4.4 and Example 4.5]. As already anticipated, here is where the regularising effect of the temporal weight ρ\rho comes into play. Indeed, we are now free to choose any ρ∈(1/p,1]\rho\in(1/p,1] and we actually take ρ<1\rho<1 by asking that ρ=1/p+ε\rho=1/p+\varepsilon, for some ε<min⁡{1−1/p,β/2}\varepsilon<\min\{1-1/p,\beta/2\}. ∥𝛙⁡(t2)∥(W2−2/p,p​(Ω))2≤C⁡(1+∥𝛙⁡(t1)∥(𝒞β​(Ω))2).\lVert\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(t_{2})\rVert_{(W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega))^{2}}\leq C(1+\lVert\boldsymbol{\uppsi}(t_{1})\rVert_{(\mathcal{C}^{\beta}(\Omega))^{2}}).

This concludes the proof of Lemma 3.11. ∎

4 Strong global well-posedness

The next step in establishing global high regularity results for the solution to (1.2)-(1.6), is to extend the maximal regularity found in the previous section to the whole time-interval (0,T)(0,T). To do this, we first need an L∞​(QT)L^{\infty}(Q_{T})-estimate for both φ\varphi and σ\sigma, which is achieved respectively by an Alikakos-Moser iterative scheme and by parabolic regularity theory. Here it is necessary to put the chemotaxis parameter χ\chi equal to 00, in order to make these arguments work. The main problem due to chemotaxis is the treatment of the cross-diffusion terms −χ​σ-\chi\sigma in (1.3) and +χ​Δ​φ+\chi\Delta\varphi in (1.4), which essentially prevent the L∞​(QT)L^{\infty}(Q_{T})-estimate, if starting only from the low regularity given by weak solutions. Indeed, we recall that the only global result available up to now is the one of Theorem 2.1; therefore we are forced to rely on that to prove global boundedness of the solutions. Subsequently, we prove Hölder-type estimates on the solutions, which, in conjunction to Lemma 3.11, allow us to extend the maximal regularity to the whole (0,T)(0,T), if χ=0\chi=0. This is then enough to prove a continuous dependence result in strong spaces, which will be the starting point of the subsequent study of the optimal control problem.

4.1 Global maximal regularity

From now on, we consider the system of equations with χ=0\chi=0, namely the system (1.7)–(1.11), which we recall here for convenience:

∂tφ−Δ​μ=P⁡(φ)​(σ−μ)−𝕙⁡(φ)​u\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi-\Delta\mu=P(\varphi)(\sigma-\mu)-\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T},
μ=A​F′​(φ)+B​a​φ−B​J∗φ\displaystyle\mu=AF^{\prime}(\varphi)+Ba\varphi-BJ\ast\varphi\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T},
∂tσ−Δ​σ=−P⁡(φ)​(σ−μ)+v\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma-\Delta\sigma=-P(\varphi)(\sigma-\mu)+v\hskip 20.00003pt in ​QT.\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}.
∂𝒏μ=∂𝒏σ=0\displaystyle\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\mu=\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\sigma=0\hskip 20.00003pt on ​ΣT,\displaystyle\text{on }\Sigma_{T},
φ⁡(0)=φ0,σ⁡(0)=σ0\displaystyle\varphi(0)=\varphi_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\sigma(0)=\sigma_{0}\hskip 20.00003pt in ​Ω.\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega.

First, we state and prove the results about the L∞​(QT)L^{\infty}(Q_{T})-estimates for φ\varphi and σ\sigma. Note that in both cases, we only need the weak regularity together with stronger assumptions on some data of the system. In particular, we have to further assume that:

  1. B7.

    P∈L∞​(ℝ)P\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}).

With this extra hypothesis we can now prove the following result.

Proposition 4.1.

Assume hypotheses A1-A9, B7 and let φ0∈L∞​(Ω)\varphi_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega). Let (φ,μ,σ)(\varphi,\mu,\sigma) be a weak solution to (1.7)–(1.11), with regularities given by Theorem 2.1.

Then, there exists a constant C>0C>0, depending only on the data of the system, such that

∥φ∥L∞​(QT)≤C.\lVert\varphi\rVert_{L^{\infty}(Q_{T})}\leq C.
Proof.

We perform an Alikakos-Moser iteration scheme, by taking some inspiration from [4, Theorem 2.1]. We start by testing (1.7) by φ​|φ|p−1\varphi\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p-1}, with p>1p>1. Note that, for this to be rigorous, one should have to consider truncated versions for the test function, i.e. φλ​|φλ|p−1\varphi_{\lambda}\lvert\varphi_{\lambda}\rvert^{p-1} with φλ=max⁡{min⁡{φ,λ},−λ}\varphi_{\lambda}=\max\{\min\{\varphi,\lambda\},-\lambda\} for any λ>0\lambda>0. In this way, φλ​|φλ|p−1\varphi_{\lambda}\lvert\varphi_{\lambda}\rvert^{p-1} would be eligible as a test function in the weak formulation. Then, one can proceed with all the estimates below and pass to the limit as λ→+∞\lambda\to+\infty to get the result. Here, with the idea of not overburdening the exposition, we proceed formally. Then, we have:

⟨φt,φ​|φ|p−1⟩V+(∇μ,∇(φ​|φ|p−1))H=(P⁡(φ)​(σ−μ),φ​|φ|p−1)H−(𝕙⁡(φ)​u,φ​|φ|p−1)H.\langle\varphi_{t},\varphi\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p-1}\rangle_{V}+(\nabla\mu,\nabla(\varphi\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p-1}))_{H}=(P(\varphi)(\sigma-\mu),\varphi\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p-1})_{H}-(\mathbbm{h}(\varphi)u,\varphi\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p-1})_{H}.

From now on, we will call the reaction term R:=σ−μR:=\sigma-\mu for simplicity and recall that by Theorem 2.1

∥R∥L2​(0,T,V)≤C.\lVert R\rVert_{L^{2}(0,T;V)}\leq C. (4.1)

Then, we rewrite the previous identity by using the explicit expression of μ\mu and we get:

Proposition 4.4.

Assume hypotheses A1-A9 and B7. Let φ0∈L∞​(Ω)\varphi_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega), σ0∈L∞​(Ω)\sigma_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega) and v∈L∞​(0,T,H)v\in L^{\infty}(0,T;H). Let (φ,μ,σ)(\varphi,\mu,\sigma) be a weak solution to (1.7)–(1.11), with regularities given by Theorem 2.1 and Propositions 4.1.

Proof.

This is just an application of maximum principle for parabolic equations. Indeed, we rewrite equation (1.9) as

σt−Δ​σ=fσ,with ​fσ=P⁡(φ)​(σ−μ)+v.\sigma_{t}-\Delta\sigma=f_{\sigma},\hskip 10.00002pt\text{with }f_{\sigma}=P(\varphi)(\sigma-\mu)+v.

Then, we can apply [31, Theorem 7.1, p. 181] with q=∞q=\infty and r=2r=2 to conclude the proof. ∎

Next, we state and prove global Hölder-type estimates for both φ\varphi and σ\sigma.

Arguing in a similar fashion, one can easily see that inequality (4.11) also holds with φ\varphi replaced by −φ-\varphi. Therefore, thanks to [31, Chapter II, Remark 7.2], we can say that φ\varphi is an element of the class ℬ⁡(Q0,T,R,γ,r,0,κ)\mathcal{B}(Q_{0,T},R,\gamma,r,0,\kappa) in the sense of [31, Chapter II, Section 7], for some γ>0\gamma>0, r>2r>2 and κ>0\kappa>0. Then, we can apply [31, Chapter II, Theorem 7.1] to infer the existence of a β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) such that

|φ⁡(x,t)−φ⁡(y,s)|≤C⁡(|x−y|β+|t−s|β2)for any ​(x,t),(y,s)∈Ω¯×[0,T].\lvert\varphi(x,t)-\varphi(y,s)\rvert\leq C\left(\lvert x-y\rvert^{\beta}+\lvert t-s\rvert^{\frac{\beta}{2}}\right)\hskip 10.00002pt\text{for any }(x,t),(y,s)\in\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T].

To get a similar estimate for σ\sigma, we argue in the same way by multiplying equation (1.9) by ζ2​σk+\zeta^{2}\sigma_{k}^{+} and integrating again on Qt0,tQ_{t_{0},t}. Here, the situation is easier since we just have the laplacian operator for σ\sigma and the reaction term and the source term can be treated essentially in the same way. Therefore, we can once again use [31, Chapter II, Theorem 7.1 and Remark 7.2] to conclude. ∎

Remark 4.6.

The result of Proposition 4.5 implies in particular that φ,σ∈𝒞0​([0,T],𝒞β​(Ω))\varphi,\sigma\in\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];\mathcal{C}^{\beta}(\Omega)) for some β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), uniformly with respect to the parameters, which means that

supt∈[0,T]∥(φ⁡(t),σ⁡(t))∥𝒞β​(Ω)2≤C.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\lVert(\varphi(t),\sigma(t))\rVert_{\mathcal{C}^{\beta}(\Omega)^{2}}\leq C.

This is what we will use in the following Theorem.

Now we are ready to prove the main results of this subsection:

Theorem 4.7.

Let ρ=1\rho=1, s=2−2p>1+Nps=2-\frac{2}{p}>1+\frac{N}{p}, with p∈(N+2,+∞)p\in(N+2,+\infty). Assume also hypotheses A1-A7 and B1-B7.

Let (φ,σ)(\varphi,\sigma) be the maximal solution to (1.7)–(1.11) in the sense of Definition 3.4 with χ=0\chi=0. Then the maximal solution is global, i.e. the maximal existence time t+=t+​(φ0,σ0,u,v)t^{+}=t^{+}(\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0},u,v) is equal to TT for any (φ0,σ0)∈M2−2/p,p(\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0})\in M^{2-2/p,p} and for any fixed u,v∈L∞​(QT)u,v\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T}).

Proof.

By Theorem 3.10, let (φ,σ)(\varphi,\sigma) be the maximal solution to (1.7)–(1.11) in the sense of Definition 3.4 with χ=0\chi=0 on I=[0,t+)I=[0,t^{+}). Assume by contradiction that t+<Tt^{+}<T, then since (φ,σ)∈𝒞⁡([0,t+),M2−2/p,p)(\varphi,\sigma)\in\mathcal{C}([0,t^{+});M^{2-2/p,p}), by definition of maximal time-interval of existence, it should hold that limt→t+∥(φ⁡(t),σ⁡(t))∥W2−2/p,p​(Ω)=+∞\lim_{t\to t^{+}}\lVert(\varphi(t),\sigma(t))\rVert_{W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega)}=+\infty. However, by Lemma 3.11 and Proposition 4.5, it follows that

supt∈[0,t+)∥(φ⁡(t),σ⁡(t))∥W2−2/p,p​(Ω)≤C⁡(1+supt∈[0,t+/2)∥(φ⁡(t),σ⁡(t))∥𝒞β​(Ω)2)≤C,\sup_{t\in[0,t^{+})}\lVert(\varphi(t),\sigma(t))\rVert_{W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega)}\leq C\left(1+\sup_{t\in[0,t^{+}/2)}\lVert(\varphi(t),\sigma(t))\rVert_{\mathcal{C}^{\beta}(\Omega)^{2}}\right)\leq C,

for β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), given by Proposition 4.5. We recall that Lemma 3.11 holds for any β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), thus here we choose exactly the one provided by Proposition 4.5. Moreover, observe that we were allowed to apply Proposition 4.5 because (φ0,σ0)∈W2−2/p,p​(Ω)↪L∞​(Ω)(\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0})\in W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{\infty}(\Omega). This contradicts the assumption, so the maximal solution can be continued to the whole interval [0,T][0,T]. ∎

In the end, we have shown the following result:

Theorem 4.8.

Assume hypotheses A1–A7, B1–B5 and B7. Assume further that

φ0,σ0∈H2​(Ω)​ with ​{∂𝒏μ⁡(0)=∂𝒏(A​F′​(φ0)+B​a​φ0−B​J∗φ0)=0∂𝒏σ0=0​on ∂Ω.\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0}\in H^{2}(\Omega)\text{ with }\begin{cases}\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\mu(0)=\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}(AF^{\prime}(\varphi_{0})+Ba\varphi_{0}-BJ\ast\varphi_{0})=0\\ \partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\sigma_{0}=0\end{cases}\text{on $\partial\Omega$}. (4.12)

Then, there exists a unique solution (φ,μ,σ)(\varphi,\mu,\sigma) to (1.7)–(1.11) such that

φ,μ,σ∈W1,6​(0,T,L6​(Ω))∩𝒞0​([0,T],W1,6​(Ω))∩L6​(0,T,W2,6​(Ω))∩𝒞0​(QT¯).\varphi,\mu,\sigma\in W^{1,6}(0,T;L^{6}(\Omega))\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];W^{1,6}(\Omega))\cap L^{6}(0,T;W^{2,6}(\Omega))\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}(\overline{Q_{T}}).

Moreover, there exists a constant C>0C>0, depending only on the parameters of the system, such that the following estimate holds:

∥(φ,μ,σ)∥(W1,6​(0,T,L6​(Ω))∩𝒞0​([0,T],W1,6​(Ω))∩L6​(0,T,W2,6​(Ω)))3≤C.\lVert(\varphi,\mu,\sigma)\rVert_{(W^{1,6}(0,T;L^{6}(\Omega))\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];W^{1,6}(\Omega))\cap L^{6}(0,T;W^{2,6}(\Omega)))^{3}}\leq C. (4.13)
Proof.

One just needs to apply Theorem 4.7 with p=6p=6, by observing that H2​(Ω)↪W2−2/p,p​(Ω)H^{2}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega) if p∈(N+2,6]p\in(N+2,6] and N≤3N\leq 3. Remark 4.9.

Observe that on initial data φ0\varphi_{0} and σ0\sigma_{0} we now assume (4.12), as it is commonly done when seeking stronger solutions for Cahn-Hilliard type equations.

Remark 4.10.

We also mention that the procedure used above also gives new regularity results for the standard non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation with constant mobility and regular potential, i.e. the system

φt−Δ​μ=0\displaystyle\varphi_{t}-\Delta\mu=0\hskip 20.00003pt in QTQ_{T},
μ=A​F′​(φ)+B​a​φ−B​J∗φ\displaystyle\mu=AF^{\prime}(\varphi)+Ba\varphi-BJ\ast\varphi\hskip 20.00003pt in QTQ_{T},
∂𝒏μ=0\displaystyle\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\mu=0\hskip 20.00003pt on ΣT\Sigma_{T},
φ⁡(0)=φ0\displaystyle\varphi(0)=\varphi_{0}\hskip 20.00003pt in Ω\Omega.

Indeed, without considering the equation for σ\sigma and by neglecting chemotaxis and forgetting the reaction and source terms, all the procedure in Sections 3 and 4 can be easily repeated. Then, under hypotheses A2–A5, B1–B2, if φ0∈W2−2/p,p​(Ω)\varphi_{0}\in W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega) for p∈(N+2,+∞)p\in(N+2,+\infty) is such that ∂nμ⁡(0)=0\partial_{n}\mu(0)=0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, one is able to prove that the unique solution to the non-local Cahn-Hilliard equation above is such that

φ,μ∈W1,p​(0,T,Lp​(Ω))∩𝒞0​([0,T],W2−2/p,p​(Ω))∩Lp​(0,T,W2,p​(Ω))∩𝒞0​(QT¯).\varphi,\mu\in W^{1,p}(0,T;L^{p}(\Omega))\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];W^{2-2/p,p}(\Omega))\cap L^{p}(0,T;W^{2,p}(\Omega))\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}(\overline{Q_{T}}).

5 Optimal control problem

From now on, we consider the initial data φ0\varphi_{0} and σ0\sigma_{0}, satisfying (4.12), fixed. As an application of the strong well-posedness that we were able to prove in Theorems 4.8 and 4.11, we consider the control problem (CP), which we recall below:

(CP) Minimise the cost functional

𝒥⁡(φ,σ,u,v)=αΩ2​∫Ω|φ⁡(T)−φΩ|2​𝑑x+αQ2​∫0T∫Ω|φ−φQ|2​𝑑x​𝑑t+βΩ2∫Ω|σ(T)−σΩ|2dx+βQ2∫0T∫Ω|σ−σQ|2dxdt+αu2∫0T∫Ω|u|2dxdt+βv2∫0T∫Ω|v|2dxdt,\begin{split}\mathcal{J}(\varphi,\sigma,u,v)&=\,\frac{\alpha_{\Omega}}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\varphi(T)-\varphi_{\Omega}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x+\frac{\alpha_{Q}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\varphi-\varphi_{Q}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\ &\quad+\frac{\beta_{\Omega}}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\sigma(T)-\sigma_{\Omega}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x+\frac{\beta_{Q}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\sigma-\sigma_{Q}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\ &\quad+\frac{\alpha_{u}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|u|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t+\frac{\beta_{v}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|v|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t,\end{split}

subject to the control constraints

u∈𝒰ad:={u∈L∞​(QT)∣umin≤u≤umax​ a.e. in ​QT},v∈𝒱ad:={v∈L∞​(QT)∣vmin≤v≤vmax​ a.e. in ​QT},\begin{split}&u\in\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}:=\{u\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})\mid u_{\text{min}}\leq u\leq u_{\text{max}}\text{ a.e.\penalty\ in }Q_{T}\},\\ &v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{ad}}:=\{v\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})\mid v_{\text{min}}\leq v\leq v_{\text{max}}\text{ a.e.\penalty\ in }Q_{T}\},\end{split}

and to the state system (1.7)-(1.11).

Regarding the parameters at play, we make the following hypotheses:

  1. C1.

    αΩ,αQ,βΩ,βQ,βu≥0\alpha_{\Omega},\alpha_{Q},\beta_{\Omega},\beta_{Q},\beta_{u}\geq 0, but not all equal to 00.

  2. C2.

    φΩ,σΩ∈L2​(Ω)\varphi_{\Omega},\sigma_{\Omega}\in L^{2}(\Omega) and φQ,σQ∈L2​(QT)\varphi_{Q},\sigma_{Q}\in L^{2}(Q_{T}).

  3. C3.

    umin,umax,vmin,vmax∈L∞​(QT)u_{\text{min}},u_{\text{max}},v_{\text{min}},v_{\text{max}}\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T}), with umin≤umaxu_{\text{min}}\leq u_{\text{max}} and vmin≤vmaxv_{\text{min}}\leq v_{\text{max}} a.e. in Ω\Omega.

  4. C4.

    P,𝕙∈𝒞2​(ℝ)∩L∞​(ℝ)P,\mathbbm{h}\in\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}).

  5. C5.

    φ0,σ0∈H2​(Ω)\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0}\in H^{2}(\Omega) with ∂𝒏(A​F′​(φ0)+B​a​φ0−B​J∗φ0)=∂𝒏σ0=0\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}(AF^{\prime}(\varphi_{0})+Ba\varphi_{0}-BJ\ast\varphi_{0})=\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\sigma_{0}=0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

Remark 5.1.

For modelling reasons, in practice one generally takes 𝕙\mathbbm{h} to be non-negative and umin≥0u_{\text{min}}\geq 0, since the radiotherapy uu should only act to decrease the tumour proliferation.

By Theorem 4.8, we know that for any (u,v)∈𝒰ad×𝒱ad(u,v)\in\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{ad}} there exists a unique strong solution (φ,μ,σ)∈𝕏(\varphi,\mu,\sigma)\in\mathbb{X} to (1.7)–(1.11), where

𝕏\displaystyle\mathbb{X} :=(W1,6​(0,T,L6​(Ω))∩𝒞0​([0,T],W1,6​(Ω))∩L6​(0,T,W2,6​(Ω)))3,\displaystyle:=\left(W^{1,6}(0,T;L^{6}(\Omega))\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];W^{1,6}(\Omega))\cap L^{6}(0,T;W^{2,6}(\Omega))\right)^{3},

therefore the optimal control problem (CP) is well-defined. Our goal is to prove existence of an optimal control and then find the first-order necessary optimality conditions. We stress that to prove such optimality conditions, we need to study the differentiability of the control-to-state operator. Hence, a strong continuous dependence estimate like (4.14) is necessary and we recall that, to prove it, we heavily relied on the global maximal regularity results. We first begin with the following existence result for optimal controls.

Theorem 5.2.

Assume hypotheses A1–A7, B1–B2 and C1–C5. Then the optimal control problem (CP) admits at least one solution (u¯,v¯)∈𝒰ad×𝒱ad(\overline{u},\overline{v})\in\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{ad}}, such that if (φ¯,μ¯,σ¯)(\overline{\varphi},\overline{\mu},\overline{\sigma}) is the solution to (1.7)–(1.11) associated to (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\overline{v}), one has that

𝒥⁡(φ¯,σ¯,u¯,v¯)=min(u,v)∈𝒰ad×𝒱ad⁡𝒥⁡(φ,σ,u,v).\mathcal{J}(\overline{\varphi},\overline{\sigma},\overline{u},\overline{v})=\min_{(u,v)\,\in\,\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{ad}}}\,\mathcal{J}(\varphi,\sigma,u,v). (5.1)
Proof.

The argument is standard and relies on the direct method of Calculus of Variations, therefore we omit it for the sake of brevity. For more details on the procedure, we refer the interested reader to [17, Theorem 4.2]. ∎

5.1 Linearised system

We now want to study Fréchet-differentiability properties of the control-to-state operator, which maps any (u,v)∈𝒰ad×𝒱ad(u,v)\in\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{ad}} into the corresponding solution of the state system. The first step consists in deriving the linearised version of system (1.7)-(1.11) and in proving its well-posedness, since it is generally the ansatz for the expression of the Fréchet derivative. Indeed, we fix a state (φ¯,μ¯,σ¯)∈𝕏(\overline{\varphi},\overline{\mu},\overline{\sigma})\in\mathbb{X} corresponding to (u¯,v¯)∈𝒰ad×𝒱ad(\overline{u},\overline{v})\in\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{ad}} and linearise near (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\overline{v}):

φ=φ¯+ξ,μ=μ¯+η,σ=σ¯+ρ,u=u¯+h,v=v¯+k,\varphi=\overline{\varphi}+\xi,\,\mu=\overline{\mu}+\eta,\,\sigma=\overline{\sigma}+\rho,\,u=\overline{u}+h,v=\overline{v}+k,

with (h,k)∈L∞​(QT)2(h,k)\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})^{2}. Then, by approximating the non-linearities at the first order of their Taylor expansion, we see that (ξ,η,ρ)(\xi,\eta,\rho) satisfy the equations:

∂tξ−Δ​η=P′​(φ¯)​(σ¯−μ¯)​ξ+P⁡(φ¯)​(ρ−η)−𝕙′​(φ¯)​u¯​ξ−𝕙⁡(φ¯)​h\displaystyle\partial_{t}\xi-\Delta\eta=P^{\prime}(\overline{\varphi})(\overline{\sigma}-\overline{\mu})\xi+P(\overline{\varphi})(\rho-\eta)-\mathbbm{h}^{\prime}(\overline{\varphi})\overline{u}\,\xi-\mathbbm{h}(\overline{\varphi})h in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}, (5.2)
η=A​F′′​(φ¯)​ξ+B​a​ξ−B​J∗ξ\displaystyle\eta=AF^{\prime\prime}(\overline{\varphi})\xi+Ba\xi-BJ\ast\xi in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}, (5.3)
∂tρ−Δ​ρ=−P′​(φ¯)​(σ¯−μ¯)​ξ−P⁡(φ¯)​(ρ−η)+k\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho-\Delta\rho=-P^{\prime}(\overline{\varphi})(\overline{\sigma}-\overline{\mu})\xi-P(\overline{\varphi})(\rho-\eta)+k in ​QT,\displaystyle\text{in }Q_{T}, (5.4)

together with boundary and initial conditions:

∂𝒏η=∂𝒏ρ=0\displaystyle\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\eta=\partial_{\boldsymbol{n}}\rho=0\hskip 20.00003pt on ​ΣT,\displaystyle\text{on }\Sigma_{T}, (5.5)
ξ⁡(0)=0,ρ⁡(0)=0\displaystyle\xi(0)=0,\hskip 10.00002pt\rho(0)=0\hskip 20.00003pt in ​Ω.\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega. (5.6)
Theorem 5.3.

Assume hypotheses A1–A7, B1–B2 and C4–C5. Let (φ¯,μ¯,σ¯)∈𝕏(\overline{\varphi},\overline{\mu},\overline{\sigma})\in\mathbb{X} be the strong solution to (1.7)–(1.11), corresponding to (u¯,v¯)∈𝒰ad×𝒱ad(\overline{u},\overline{v})\in\mathcal{U}_{\text{ad}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{ad}}. Then, for any (h,k)∈L2​(0,T,H)×L2​(0,T,H)(h,k)\in L^{2}(0,T;H)\times L^{2}(0,T;H), the linearised system (5.2)–(5.6) admits a unique weak solution, which is uniformly bounded in the following spaces
